<description>
This migrates the headers presync parameters (`commitment_period` and `redownload_buffer_size`) from being precomputed chainparams to being computed at runtime during startup. This has as advantages:
* Less work for maintainers that need to occasionally run the current `contrib/devtools/headerssync-params.py` script.
* Less room for mistakes in that process.
* Automatically adapts based on time (as opposed to needing to predict the lifetime of the software).

To achieve this, the parameter search algorithm is implemented in C++. It is simpler, because it does not attempt to model the fact that the attacker is forced to submit their headers in batches of 2000. The old Python code did that, but actually got it (slightly) wrong by missing the fact that attackers are capable of strategically deciding to stop the attack in the middle of a batch (found by darosior).

Unit tests and fuzz tests are added, and at the end the old Python code is deleted.
</description>

Similarly to #35208, could an incorrect startup clock leave us with an inflated memory allowance after the clock is corrected? Fresh nodes seem to skip the clock check against the stored chain tip for some reason: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/02d1084eba30de70c45eeaee77312fd417f79bd8/src/node/chainstate.cpp#L249-L255

According to my clanker, starting with a clock near the Unix epoch and correcting it before headers sync could leave the per-peer commitment allowance about 50x higher than intended - could we defer the estimate after the clock checks?
